#### About Al-Ghazali

Abū Ḥāmid al-Ghazālī (1058–1111) taught law and theology in Baghdad before a crisis of certainty drove him from public office into Sufi practice and writing. He mastered the falāsifa well enough to attack their metaphysics in The Incoherence of the Philosophers, then narrated his own epistemic itinerary in Deliverance from Error.

### Interpretation

Al-Ghazali is stating a requirement of his ethics rather than praising balance. Knowledge without action is vain because, in his account, the purpose of knowing the good is to do it, so unused knowledge is a failure of its own point. Action without knowledge is dangerous because effort unguided by understanding can do harm while feeling righteous. The two clauses are asymmetric: the first is wasted, the second is destructive.

#### Why it matters

It gives a sharper standard than "practice what you preach": check whether what you know has changed what you do, and separately, whether what you are doing rests on anything you have examined.

### Questions readers arrive with

#### What is the source of the quotation “Knowledge without action is vanity, and action without…”?

“Knowledge without action is vanity, and action without…” comes from Iḥyāʾ ʿUlūm al-Dīn et al., attributed to Al-Ghazali.

#### What does Al-Ghazali mean by knowledge?

Epistemology asks whether knowledge is justified true belief, reliable tracking of the world, or something else; it also asks how perception, testimony, memory, and reason contribute. This passage enters that discussion through knowledge, practice, cultivation.
